title: Why waves break as they reach the shore
description: Out at sea a wave is a smooth swell. Near the beach it rears up, curls and crashes. The change happens because the wave starts to feel the bottom.

body.heading: A wave that touches the bottom
paragraphs: In deep water a wave moves through water that barely travels with it — the energy passes along while the water mostly circles in place. When the water gets shallower than about half the wave's length, the bottom of the wave starts to drag against the seabed.
The drag slows the wave's base while its top keeps moving at the old speed. The wave grows steeper and taller as the water behind piles into the slowing front.

body.heading: The curl and the crash
paragraphs: Eventually the top of the wave is leaning so far forward, moving faster than the base beneath it, that it can no longer stand. It topples over — the breaking surfers ride and beachgoers hear as surf.
Gentle slopes make waves spill gradually in white foam; steep shores make them plunge in a single dramatic curl. The beach itself decides how its waves break.

takeaway: Waves break because shallow water drags at their base while the top races on, until the crest topples forward into surf.
